proposal.hypothesis: The organizers' FM baseline, ported to the DataAPI. The incumbent every candidate is measured against.

node.change_summary: Replaced pointwise logistic-regression loss with a per-user-group listwise softmax cross-entropy (ListNet-style), computed vectorized via np.reduceat over contiguous user-grouped batches, with zero gradient for non-discriminative (all-pos/all-neg) groups.

proposal.hypothesis: The baseline trains with pointwise binary cross-entropy, which optimizes each impression's absolute predicted probability independently. But the metric (GAUC, nDCG@5) only cares about the *within-user ordering* of impressions — a user's group-level score is invariant to any monotone rescaling that preserves order. Pointwise logloss spends gradient budget calibrating scores for the 5.1%+2.3%=7.4% of train users whose groups are all-negative or all-positive (which the metric literally cannot see, since GAUC excludes them and nDCG@5 gives them a fixed 0 regardless of order), diluting the signal available for the 92.7% "discriminative" users where ordering actually matters. Replacing the pointwise loss with a per-user listwise softmax cross-entropy (ListNet-style: softmax the model's scores within each user's impression group, cross-entropy against the normalized label distribution) directly targets ranking within groups, and its gradient is naturally zero for non-discriminative groups (npos=0 or npos=n), so 100% of the gradient signal concentrates exactly where GAUC/nDCG can register the effect. I expect this to move GAUC more than nDCG@5 since GAUC's scope is literally the discriminative-user population this loss privileges, and predict primary improves by roughly +0.006 on valid.
proposal.grounding: splits.train.user_composition (discriminative_pct 92.7%, all_negative_pct 5.1%, all_positive_pct 2.3%) combined with the metric definition (GAUC only scores 0<positives<impressions users; nDCG@5 gives all-negative users a fixed 0 regardless of order)

node.change_summary: Added a leave-one-out, Bayesian-shrunk user x author historical long_view-rate deviation feature (computed from train history only, causal for valid/test) as an extra learned linear term in the FM logit, on top of the unchanged 5-field baseline FM.

proposal.hypothesis: The FM baseline only sees `user_id`, `video_id`, `author_id`, `tab`, `duration_bucket` as separate fields, so the only way a user's specific taste can affect the ranking of one candidate over another in her group is through the learned `user_id x author_id` interaction inside the FM's low-rank embedding -- and that interaction is squeezed through the same rank-16 space as every other pairwise term (embedding-capacity was already shown not to be the bottleneck at k=8/16/32). Nothing in the current pipeline uses the user's actual behavioural sequence at all, and per the profile the median user has 31 prior train impressions (p90=97) -- enough history to build a direct, non-decomposable user x item-side statistic instead of relying on the embedding to discover it. I will add one engineered feature per row: a smoothed, leave-one-out (for train) "user x author historical affinity" = (this user's empirical long_view rate on this author's videos, Bayesian-shrunk toward the author's global rate) minus the author's global rate. This is a genuine cross term -- it is jointly a function of (user, author), not decomposable into a pure user term times a pure item term, so unlike dead end #3 (`item_pop x user_bias`) it does not cancel arithmetically inside a user's group: two candidates by different authors get different values of this feature for the same user, so it can change their relative order. I feed it into the FM's logit as an extra learned linear term alongside the existing embedding-based interactions. I expect a small but real primary gain concentrated in GAUC (where discriminative users with repeat-author exposure benefit) since author_id already varies in ~99% of impression groups, so this feature has room to act almost everywhere; I predict primary improves by about +0.0018 on valid, mostly through GAUC.
proposal.grounding: train_history_per_user (median 31, p90 97 prior impressions per user) combined with within_user_variance.author_id=0.991

node.change_summary: Added an auxiliary BPR pairwise loss on sampled within-user (pos,neg) pairs on top of the existing pointwise logloss, so gradient is explicitly steered away from per-user-constant terms (bias, user linear weight) that cancel out of within-user ranking, toward terms that actually vary inside a group.

proposal.hypothesis: The FM baseline trains with pointwise logloss, whose gradient is driven by matching each row's absolute predicted probability to the global positive rate. Two of its components — the scalar bias `b` and the linear weight `W[user_id]` — are, by construction, constant across every impression inside one user's group (since `user_id` doesn't vary within a group). The evaluation metric (GAUC/nDCG) only ever compares scores *within* a group, so any gradient spent moving these per-user-constant terms toward the "right" absolute calibration produces literally zero change in the score — it is capacity and gradient spent on something the metric discards by construction (`within_user_variance`: "a per-user constant cancels out of that user's ordering exactly"). The ledger already shows that fully *replacing* pointwise logloss with a listwise softmax over the whole group hurt (`loss/listwise_softmax_ce`, Δ −0.0029), likely because normalizing over full, highly variable-length groups (p10=5 to p90=97 impressions/user) destabilizes training and removing the pointwise calibration term entirely throws away a stabilizing anchor. Instead, I add a *pairwise BPR term as an auxiliary loss* on top of the existing pointwise logloss, applied only to sampled within-group (positive, negative) pairs. The BPR gradient on the bias `b` sums to exactly zero across a pos/neg pair by construction (its contribution to z_pos and z_neg cancels algebraically), so it explicitly redirects gradient away from the per-user-constant terms and into the terms that vary within a group (`video_id`, `author_id`, `tab`, `dur_bucket`, and their FM interactions with `user_id`) — the only place ranking signal can live. Because the pointwise term is retained, training stability is preserved while the auxiliary pairwise term supplies gradient that is, by construction, aligned with what the metric actually rewards. I predict a modest but real gain over the milder failure mode of the pure listwise replacement, roughly +0.0025 on primary, concentrated in GAUC (which is the component most sensitive to within-group ordering of moderate-size groups) with nDCG@5 roughly flat.
